propositions.text: The appellant is Jennifer Virgo, appealing a Federal Court order from December 17, 2018.
There is a serious problem with the appeal that requires action due to a vexatious litigant order breach.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Jennifer Virgo appeals a Federal Court order but notes a serious problem with the appeal involving a vexatious litigant order breach.

propositions.text: Jennifer Virgo is spouse of Ade Olumide, who was declared a vexatious litigant by this Court in 2017.
Canada v. Olumide, 2017 FCA 42 declared Ade Olumide a vexatious litigant prohibiting new proceedings without leave.
The vexatious litigant order prohibits Ade Olumide from starting new proceedings without leave, directly or through others.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains Jennifer Virgo is Ade Olumide's spouse, who is a vexatious litigant prohibited from starting new proceedings without leave.

propositions.text: Ade Olumide is litigating through Jennifer Virgo without seeking leave, breaching the vexatious litigant order.
The breach of the vexatious litigant order is flagrant.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Ade Olumide is litigating through Jennifer Virgo without leave, flagrantly breaching the vexatious litigant order.

propositions.text: The Prothonotary and Federal Court found Jennifer Virgo's name disguises Ade Olumide as the directing mind behind the proceedings.
These findings are not challenged in this Court.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes earlier decisions found Jennifer Virgo's name disguises Ade Olumide's control, and these findings are unchallenged here.

propositions.text: The situation is worse than earlier findings; Ade Olumide is the true appellant, not Jennifer Virgo.
Jennifer Virgo has no interest in the appeal; documents filed are authored by Ade Olumide.
Documents show Ade Olumide's authorship by style and explicit acknowledgment.
Ade Olumide started a new proceeding without leave, breaching the vexatious litigant order by acting through others.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Ade Olumide is the true appellant, with documents authored by him, breaching the vexatious litigant order by acting through others.

propositions.text: Serious consequences are possible; background shows the Court gave Ade Olumide and Jennifer Virgo full opportunity to explain and address conduct.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes serious consequences and that Ade Olumide and Jennifer Virgo had full opportunity to explain their conduct.

propositions.text: Four weeks ago, a motion by Jennifer Virgo raised suspicion that Ade Olumide was litigating through her, contrary to the vexatious litigant order.
The respondent highlighted Ade Olumide's involvement in previous motions in this appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The court states a recent motion by Jennifer Virgo raised suspicion of Ade Olumide litigating through her, as the respondent noted.

propositions.text: Rule 74 requires removal of documents filed contrary to Court orders, but only after submissions and if warranted.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains Rule 74 requires removal of documents filed contrary to Court orders after submissions and if warranted.

propositions.text: The Court has plenary powers to restrain abuses and stop meritless proceedings, supported by Federal Courts Act and case law.

paragraphs.summary: The court states it has plenary powers to restrain abuses and stop meritless proceedings under the Federal Courts Act and case law.

propositions.text: The Court issued a direction stating preliminary view that the appeal breaches the vexatious litigant order.
The Court invited parties to file evidence and representations addressing five specific questions about the appeal and standing.

paragraphs.summary: The court issued a direction on the vexatious litigant breach and invited parties to address five questions about the appeal and standing.

propositions.text: Jennifer Virgo and Ade Olumide did not file evidence or representations to rebut the Court's preliminary view.
The Attorney General filed representations; Jennifer Virgo and Ade Olumide did not reply.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes Jennifer Virgo and Ade Olumide did not file evidence or reply, but the Attorney General filed representations.

propositions.text: The Court is satisfied Jennifer Virgo and Ade Olumide had full and fair opportunity to address the matter.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes Jennifer Virgo and Ade Olumide had full and fair opportunity to address the matter.

propositions.text: Whether this matter can be decided by one judge or requires three judges.
One judge can deal with this matter for the following reasons.

paragraphs.summary: The court raises and answers the issue that one judge can decide this matter.

propositions.text: Section 16 of the Federal Courts Act requires three judges for appeals unless otherwise provided.
The matter before the Court is not a hearing of an appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The court states section 16 requires three judges for appeals but finds this matter is not a hearing of an appeal.

propositions.text: Section 40 allows a single judge to make a vexatious litigant order and address non-compliance.
A single judge can address breaches and amend or supplement the vexatious litigant order.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains a single judge can make and address breaches of vexatious litigant orders under section 40.

propositions.text: Rule 74 can remove the notice of appeal and close the file, effectively terminating the appeal.
Such an order ensures compliance with the vexatious litigant order and does not dispose of the appeal on its merits.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Rule 74 can terminate the appeal to ensure compliance but does not decide the appeal's merits.

propositions.text: Using Rule 74 to terminate an appeal for lack of jurisdiction differs from its use here to enforce a vexatious litigant order.
Cases Rock-St Laurent and Wong illustrate Rule 74 use to terminate appeals for jurisdictional reasons.

paragraphs.summary: The court distinguishes Rule 74 use here from cases where it terminates appeals for lack of jurisdiction.

propositions.text: Potential consequences of breaching the vexatious litigant order are severe in a free society.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the severe potential consequences of breaching the vexatious litigant order.

propositions.text: The Court can start contempt proceedings against Ade Olumide for breaching the vexatious litigant order immediately and on its own initiative.
Contempt consequences include imprisonment, fines, orders, property seizure, and costs liability under Rules 466-472.

paragraphs.summary: The court states it can start contempt proceedings against Ade Olumide with severe possible penalties under court rules.

propositions.text: Due to the importance of vexatious litigant orders and the flagrant breach, the Court is certain it can start contempt proceedings now.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds it can start contempt proceedings now given the importance of vexatious litigant orders and the flagrant breach.

propositions.text: Contempt proceedings can be started but their initiation is discretionary.

paragraphs.summary: The court states contempt proceedings can be started but their initiation is discretionary.

propositions.text: The Court examined all decisions against Ade Olumide across Canada, including vexatious litigant declarations.
All jurisdictions have contempt provisions similar to this Court's.
Ade Olumide was told about possible contempt proceedings but not about serious consequences in detail.

paragraphs.summary: The court examined all decisions against Ade Olumide and found he was told about contempt but not serious consequences.

propositions.text: This case is a close call but a clear, strong warning about serious consequences is appropriate.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds this case close but warrants a clear, strong warning about serious consequences.

propositions.text: Ade Olumide is warned that recurrence of similar conduct will lead to contempt proceedings.
Jennifer Virgo is warned that complicity in breach may lead to contempt proceedings against her.
If found guilty of contempt, severe consequences including imprisonment and fines apply.

paragraphs.summary: The court warns Ade Olumide and Jennifer Virgo about contempt proceedings and severe consequences if found guilty.

propositions.text: The Court chose to write widely accessible reasons rather than a less-accessible speaking order and asks why.

paragraphs.summary: The court questions why it chose to write widely accessible reasons instead of a speaking order.

propositions.text: The Court wants judges and Prothonotaries in Federal and other courts to know Ade Olumide and Jennifer Virgo received a strong warning.
Ade Olumide and Jennifer Virgo now know contempt proceedings can be easily started and have serious consequences.
Long imprisonment and substantial fines are real possibilities for contempt.
If Ade Olumide or Jennifer Virgo ignore this warning, they risk dangerous proceedings in future.

paragraphs.summary: The court states judges and officers know Ade Olumide and Jennifer Virgo received a strong warning about contempt and consequences.

propositions.text: The respondent complained Ade Olumide breached the vexatious litigant order.
The respondent was appropriate to complain about the breach.
The Court should have considered the respondent's complaint and acted sooner but did not criticize the delay.
After receiving the notice of appeal, the respondent could have forced the Court to deal with the breach under Rule 74 or plenary power.

paragraphs.summary: The respondent complained about Ade Olumide's breach; the court finds the complaint appropriate and notes the respondent could have forced earlier action.

propositions.text: Multiple means exist to summarily terminate illegitimate or doomed proceedings in this Court.
Fabrikant No. 1 and Fabrikant No. 2 cases list such means.
Cases like Canada v. J.P. Morgan, Lee v. Canada, and Forner v. PIPSC show general power to quash.
Many cases show this Court's plenary jurisdiction is often invoked and exercised.

paragraphs.summary: The court states multiple means exist to terminate illegitimate proceedings, citing Fabrikant cases and others showing plenary power use.

propositions.text: Respondents and judges should prioritize early quashing of illegitimate or hopeless proceedings to free resources.
Fabrikant No. 2 para. 25 underscores resource issues in the Court.
Court's legal complement lags population growth; complex cases compete for limited docket space.
Proactive litigation management aims to root out unmeritorious cases early and simplify others.
Resource issues remain pressing, impairing timely access to justice.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds early quashing of illegitimate cases is vital due to resource issues impairing timely justice.

propositions.text: Given available tools and Supreme Court encouragement, it is baffling why illegitimate proceedings persist in the court system.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds it baffling that illegitimate proceedings persist despite available tools and Supreme Court encouragement.

propositions.text: The appeal and filing of the notice of appeal violate the vexatious litigant order.
Under Rule 74 and plenary power, the notice of appeal is removed and the file closed.
The respondent does not seek global costs of the appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The court orders removal of the notice of appeal and file closure for vexatious litigant order breach; respondent does not seek costs.

propositions.text: The respondent requests Ade Olumide be prohibited from representing or conducting litigation for others.
This request goes beyond the vexatious litigant order's prohibition on starting new proceedings without leave.
The requested order would prevent Ade Olumide from conducting litigation for others regardless of interest.

paragraphs.summary: The respondent requests a broader prohibition on Ade Olumide representing others; the court finds it exceeds the vexatious litigant order.

propositions.text: Under plenary power and Rule 55, the court would make the requested order prohibiting Ade Olumide from conducting litigation for others without leave.
Rule 119 prohibits Ade Olumide from representing others without leave of the Court.
The requested order is broader than Rule 119 but justified given Ade Olumide's vexatious litigant status and breaches.

paragraphs.summary: The court would order Ade Olumide prohibited from conducting litigation for others without leave, broader than Rule 119 but justified.

propositions.text: A motion within this appeal led the Court to call for submissions under Rule 74.
The Court has not decided this motion and will dismiss it as the appeal no longer exists.
The respondent seeks costs for the motion.
The court would dismiss the motion with costs to the respondent.

paragraphs.summary: The court will dismiss the motion as the appeal ends and grant costs to the respondent.
